subject: ela
intro: Each problem includes a full informational passage. Read it carefully, then cite the strongest, most relevant evidence and explain how it supports the claim. Use the exact words from the passage when you quote, and keep explanations in your own words.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"For most of history, the only way to send a message across an ocean was to put a letter on a ship and wait weeks for a reply. That changed in 1858, when crews on two warships unspooled a copper cable across the floor of the Atlantic, linking Ireland to Newfoundland. The first messages crackled through in minutes instead of weeks, and crowds celebrated in the streets. The triumph did not last. The cable's insulation was thin, the voltage pushed through it was far too high, and within a few weeks the line went dead. Engineers spent the next eight years studying what had gone wrong. When a new cable was laid in 1866, it used thicker insulation, gentler signals, and stronger materials. That line stayed in service for decades, and within a generation cables crossed every major ocean."

A writer claims: The 1858 cable failed mainly because of how it was built and operated, not because the idea of an undersea cable was impossible. Quote the one sentence that gives the strongest support for this claim, and explain how it supports the claim.
items.answer: Strongest evidence: "The cable's insulation was thin, the voltage pushed through it was far too high, and within a few weeks the line went dead." This sentence names specific construction and operation problems (thin insulation, too much voltage) that caused the failure, which supports the claim that the failure came from how the cable was built and run, not from the idea itself.

steps: Identify the claim: the 1858 failure was about build and operation, not the basic idea.
Scan for a sentence that names causes of the failure rather than just describing the celebration or the later success.
The sentence about thin insulation and too-high voltage lists concrete build and operation flaws.
Connect it: because the named problems are about materials and handling, the evidence shows the idea could work once those flaws were fixed, which the 1866 cable confirms.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"Sea otters spend nearly their whole lives in cold coastal water, yet they have no blubber to keep warm. Instead, they rely on the densest fur of any animal, packed so tightly that water never reaches their skin. To keep that fur working, an otter grooms constantly, trapping a layer of air against its body. This grooming has a hidden cost. An otter must eat about a quarter of its body weight in food every day just to fuel the heat its body loses to the water. Much of that food is sea urchins. Where otters thrive, urchin numbers stay low, and the kelp forests the urchins would have eaten grow thick and tall. Those kelp forests shelter fish, crabs, and snails. When otters disappear, urchins multiply and strip the kelp down to bare rock."

Which statement below is an INFERENCE drawn from the passage rather than something the text states directly? Explain how the passage supports it.
items.answer: Inference: "Sea otters help keep entire kelp forest communities alive." The text never says this directly, but it states that otters keep urchin numbers low, that low urchin numbers let kelp grow thick, and that kelp forests shelter fish, crabs, and snails. Combining these stated facts leads to the inference that otters help keep the whole community alive.

steps: An inference is a reasonable conclusion the text does not state in so many words.
The passage directly states otters eat urchins, low urchins let kelp grow, and kelp shelters other animals.
It never directly states that otters keep the whole community alive; that is a conclusion built from several facts.
Linking the chain of stated facts supports the inference about the community.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"In 1845, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards. In the first ward, where doctors delivered babies, far more mothers died of fever than in the second ward, run by midwives. Semmelweis searched for a difference between the wards. He noticed that the doctors often came straight from examining dead bodies, while the midwives did not. He guessed that the doctors were carrying something invisible on their hands. When he ordered the doctors to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before each delivery, the death rate in the first ward fell sharply. Yet many other doctors refused to believe him, partly because no one had yet discovered germs, and partly because the idea that healers were spreading death was insulting to them. Semmelweis was pushed out of his job, and only years later did science prove him right."

A reader claims: Semmelweis's hand washing rule was the reason the first ward improved. Three quotations appear below. Choose the one that gives the STRONGEST direct support for that claim and explain why it is stronger than the others.

Quotation X: "In 1845, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards."
Quotation Y: "When he ordered the doctors to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before each delivery, the death rate in the first ward fell sharply."
Quotation Z: "Semmelweis was pushed out of his job, and only years later did science prove him right."
items.answer: Strongest: Quotation Y, "When he ordered the doctors to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before each delivery, the death rate in the first ward fell sharply." It directly links the hand washing rule to the drop in deaths, which is exactly the claim. Quotation X only sets the scene, and Quotation Z is about his career and later vindication, not about the cause of the ward's improvement.

steps: The claim is about cause: hand washing caused the first ward to improve.
Quotation Y states the rule and the falling death rate together, showing the cause and effect.
Quotation X gives background only and proves nothing about the cause.
Quotation Z is true but off claim; it describes his fate, not why the ward improved.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"A lightning bolt is one of the hottest things on Earth. In the instant it flashes, the air inside the bolt can reach nearly 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than the surface of the sun. That sudden heat makes the air expand so fast that it explodes outward, creating the sound we call thunder. Because light travels far faster than sound, we see the flash almost instantly but hear the thunder later. You can estimate how far away a storm is by counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder. Every five seconds of delay means the lightning struck about one mile away. If the flash and the thunder arrive together, the storm is directly overhead and most dangerous. As a storm moves off, the gap between flash and thunder grows longer."

The author wants the reader to understand WHY thunder is heard after the lightning is seen. Quote the single sentence that best explains this, and put the reason in your own words.
items.answer: Best evidence: "Because light travels far faster than sound, we see the flash almost instantly but hear the thunder later." In my own words, light reaches our eyes much sooner than sound reaches our ears, so the flash is seen first and the thunder, which travels slower, arrives afterward.

steps: The question asks why thunder comes after the lightning is seen.
Locate the sentence that gives the reason rather than describing temperature or distance.
The sentence about light traveling faster than sound states the cause directly.
Restate the cause: faster light is seen first, slower sound is heard later.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"The dodo was a large, flightless bird that lived only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. For thousands of years it had no natural enemies there, so it had no fear of anything and built its nests on the open ground. When sailors first reached the island in the late 1500s, they found the birds easy to approach and easy to catch. But the sailors did more than hunt the dodos. They brought pigs, rats, monkeys, and dogs ashore, and these animals ate the dodo's eggs and chicks straight from the unprotected nests. The forests where dodos fed were also cleared. Within less than a century of the sailors' arrival, the dodo was gone forever. Today the bird survives only in old drawings and a few scattered bones."

A student writes: "The dodo went extinct only because hunters ate too many of them." Using the passage, decide whether this is fully supported, and quote the evidence that complicates or corrects it.
items.answer: The claim is not fully supported. Evidence that corrects it: "They brought pigs, rats, monkeys, and dogs ashore, and these animals ate the dodo's eggs and chicks straight from the unprotected nests." The passage shows that introduced animals destroying eggs and chicks, plus the clearing of forests, also drove the extinction, so hunting was not the only cause.

steps: Test the claim that hunting alone caused extinction.
Search the passage for other causes the text names.
The text states introduced animals ate eggs and chicks and that forests were cleared.
These additional causes show the single-cause claim is too narrow.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all ocean species. A reef is not a single creature but a city built by millions of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp pulls minerals from the seawater to build a hard cup around itself, and over centuries these cups pile into the reef. Living inside the polyps are even smaller partners, colorful algae that make food from sunlight and share it with their hosts. This partnership only works in warm, clear, shallow water. When the water grows too warm, the polyps push the algae out, lose their color, and begin to starve. Scientists call this bleaching. A reef can recover if the water cools again quickly, but if the heat lasts too long, the reef dies and the animals that depended on it scatter or perish."

Which detail best supports the inference that coral reefs are far more important to ocean life than their small size would suggest? Explain the link.
items.answer: Best evidence: "Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all ocean species." This detail contrasts the reef's tiny area with the huge share of species it supports, which directly backs the inference that reefs matter far more than their size suggests.

steps: The inference is that reefs are more important than their small size implies.
Look for a detail that compares size to importance.
The opening sentence pairs less than one percent of the floor with a quarter of all species.
That size-versus-impact contrast directly supports the inference.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"In the 1930s, years of plowing up the grasslands of the American Plains left the soil loose and bare. When a long drought struck, there were no deep grass roots left to hold the dirt in place. Strong winds lifted the dry topsoil into towering clouds that rolled across whole states. People called these storms black blizzards. The dust buried fences, darkened the sky at midday, and crept through the cracks of sealed houses. Many farm families lost everything and packed up to search for work elsewhere. In response, the government planted long rows of trees to slow the wind and taught farmers methods that kept roots in the ground year round. Slowly the land began to heal. The disaster taught the country a hard lesson about how farming can wreck the very soil it depends on."

The author argues that human farming choices, not just the weather, caused the dust storms. Choose the strongest evidence, quote it, and explain why a sentence about the wind or the drought alone would be weaker support.
items.answer: Strongest evidence: "In the 1930s, years of plowing up the grasslands of the American Plains left the soil loose and bare." It names a human choice, plowing, as what left the soil exposed, directly supporting the claim that farming caused the storms. A sentence about the wind or drought alone would be weaker because wind and drought are natural and do not show the human role; the plowing is what made the natural events so destructive.

steps: The claim blames human farming choices, not weather alone.
Find the sentence that names a human action behind the bare soil.
The plowing sentence states the human cause directly.
Wind or drought sentences describe nature, not the human choice, so they support the claim less well.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"The Wright brothers did not invent the airplane in a single lucky flight. For years they studied how birds tilted their wings to turn and steer. They built a wind tunnel, a box with a fan, and tested hundreds of small wing shapes inside it to learn which lifted best. They flew large kites and gliders again and again, crashing many times and changing their design after each crash. Only after this slow testing did they add an engine. On December 17, 1903, their powered machine lifted off and flew for twelve seconds. Newspapers barely noticed at first. The brothers kept improving the craft, and within a few years their planes could circle in the air for over half an hour."

Four statements appear below. Identify the ONE that is something the text states EXPLICITLY (not an inference), and briefly explain how you can tell.

W) The Wright brothers were more patient than other inventors of their time.
X) Careful testing was the key to the brothers' success.
Y) They built a wind tunnel and tested hundreds of small wing shapes inside it.
Z) The public should have paid more attention to the first flight.
items.answer: Explicit statement: Y, "They built a wind tunnel, a box with a fan, and tested hundreds of small wing shapes inside it." The passage states this fact word for word. W, X, and Z are inferences or opinions the reader draws; the text never directly says the brothers were more patient than others, that testing was the key, or that the public should have paid more attention.

steps: Explicit means the text says it in its own words; inference is a conclusion the reader builds.
Statement Y matches a sentence in the passage directly.
W and Z are judgments the text never states outright.
X is a reasonable conclusion but not directly stated, so it is an inference, not explicit.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"Honeybees survive winter as a team. When the temperature outside drops, the bees do not hibernate or fly south. Instead, they crowd together into a tight ball inside the hive, with the queen at the center. The bees on the outside of the ball form a kind of living blanket, while the bees inside shiver their flight muscles without moving their wings. This shivering produces heat, and the cluster can stay warm even when snow covers the hive. The bees take turns rotating from the chilly outer edge to the warm middle, so no single bee freezes. To fuel all this shivering, the colony slowly eats the honey it stored during summer. A hive that ran out of honey before spring will not survive the cold."

A reader infers that a honeybee colony's summer work and its winter survival are connected. Quote the single best detail supporting this inference and explain the connection.
items.answer: Best evidence: "To fuel all this shivering, the colony slowly eats the honey it stored during summer." This detail links the summer activity, storing honey, to winter survival, because the stored honey is the fuel the bees burn to make heat and stay alive through the cold.

steps: The inference connects summer work to winter survival.
Find the detail that ties the two seasons together.
The sentence about eating honey stored during summer joins the seasons.
Explain: summer honey becomes the winter fuel, so the two are connected.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"For centuries, mapmakers in Europe left huge blank spaces in the middle of Africa, simply because they had no reliable information about it. In the 1800s, explorers pushed up the great rivers to fill in those blanks, and one of the longest searches was for the source of the Nile. The Nile runs north for over four thousand miles before reaching the sea, but no one in Europe knew where it began. Several expeditions ended in failure, with members lost to disease, hunger, or hostile terrain. In 1858, an explorer named John Speke reached a vast inland lake and argued it was the source. Other geographers disagreed loudly, and the debate lasted for years. Later expeditions confirmed that the lake Speke found did feed the river. The blank spaces on the maps slowly filled in, though often at a terrible human cost."

The central idea of this passage is best described as the difficult, costly effort to map unknown regions. Which sentence functions as a small supporting example rather than the central idea itself? Quote it and explain the difference.
items.answer: Supporting example: "In 1858, an explorer named John Speke reached a vast inland lake and argued it was the source." This is one specific instance of the larger effort, not the main point. The central idea is the broad, costly struggle to map unknown regions; Speke's lake is just one example used to illustrate that struggle.

steps: The central idea is the broad, costly effort to map unknown lands.
A supporting example is one narrow instance that illustrates the bigger point.
The sentence about Speke reaching the lake is a single specific event.
It illustrates the larger effort rather than stating the main idea, so it is a supporting example.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"Most volcanoes erupt with rivers of glowing lava, but some are far more dangerous in a quieter way. A few volcanoes sit on top of enormous chambers of magma so large that scientists call them supervolcanoes. One lies beneath Yellowstone National Park. When such a volcano erupted in the distant past, it did not just bury the nearby land. It threw so much ash into the sky that the cloud blocked sunlight across much of the planet. With less sunlight reaching the ground, temperatures fell and plants struggled to grow for years. Animals that depended on those plants died in large numbers far from the volcano itself. Scientists watch Yellowstone closely, but they stress that such an eruption is extremely rare and that warning signs would likely appear long before one occurred."

A writer claims: A supervolcano can harm living things thousands of miles from the eruption. Quote the strongest supporting detail and explain how it reaches beyond the volcano.
items.answer: Strongest evidence: "It threw so much ash into the sky that the cloud blocked sunlight across much of the planet." This shows the eruption's effect spreading worldwide by blocking sunlight, which reaches far beyond the volcano. The blocked sunlight then cooled the planet and killed distant plants and animals, supporting the claim about harm thousands of miles away.

steps: The claim is about harm far from the eruption site.
Look for a detail describing an effect that travels a long distance.
The ash cloud blocking sunlight across the planet is a planet-wide effect.
Connect it: less sunlight cooled distant regions and killed faraway life, supporting the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"The first public libraries that anyone could use for free were a radical idea. Before them, books were expensive, and reading was mostly a privilege of the wealthy. A reformer named Andrew Carnegie, who had grown rich in the steel industry, decided to spend much of his fortune building libraries. He paid for the buildings in town after town, on one firm condition: each town had to agree to pay for the books and the staff with its own taxes. Carnegie believed a library should belong to the whole community, not to one donor. Between 1883 and 1929, his money built more than 2,500 libraries around the world. Many of those buildings still stand and still lend books today. Carnegie once said that a free library was the best gift he could give a community, because it let anyone, rich or poor, improve themselves."

Which quotation best supports the inference that Carnegie wanted the libraries to be owned and sustained by the communities themselves, not just handed to them? Explain why a weaker quotation about the number of libraries would not support this as well.
items.answer: Best evidence: "He paid for the buildings in town after town, on one firm condition: each town had to agree to pay for the books and the staff with its own taxes." The condition that towns fund books and staff shows he wanted communities to own and sustain the libraries. A quotation about the 2,500 libraries only shows how many he built, not that he wanted communities to take responsibility for them, so it would support the inference less well.

steps: The inference is that Carnegie wanted communities to own and sustain the libraries.
Find the detail showing community responsibility.
The condition that towns pay for books and staff shows shared ownership.
A count of libraries shows scale, not ownership intent, so it is weaker support.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"Some plants cannot get all the nutrients they need from the thin, poor soil where they grow. In a bog, where the ground is wet and low in nitrogen, the Venus flytrap solves this problem in a startling way. Its leaves form pairs of hinged pads lined with tiny trigger hairs. When an insect crawls across a pad and touches two hairs in a row, or one hair twice, the trap snaps shut in less than a second. The plant does not waste energy snapping at raindrops or bits of dirt, which is why it waits for two touches before closing. Once the trap is shut, the plant releases juices that slowly break the insect down, drawing out the nitrogen the soil could not provide. After about a week the trap reopens, empty, ready to catch again. In this way the flytrap turns a hunting strategy into a substitute for rich soil."

The author suggests the flytrap's two-touch trigger is not an accident but a useful adaptation. Quote the sentence that best supports this, and explain the reasoning that links it to the claim.
items.answer: Best evidence: "The plant does not waste energy snapping at raindrops or bits of dirt, which is why it waits for two touches before closing." This shows the two-touch rule has a purpose: it stops the plant from wasting energy on false alarms. That purpose links the trigger to the claim that it is a useful adaptation rather than an accident.

steps: The claim is that the two-touch trigger is a useful adaptation, not random.
Find the sentence that gives a reason for the two-touch rule.
The sentence about not wasting energy explains the purpose of waiting for two touches.
A feature that saves energy and serves a purpose is an adaptation, which supports the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"When a big earthquake strikes near the coast, the danger is not over when the shaking stops. The quake can shove a huge slab of the seafloor upward or downward in an instant. That sudden movement pushes the whole column of water above it, sending out waves that race across the open ocean at the speed of a jet plane. In deep water these waves are low and easy to miss, sometimes only a foot or two high. But as they reach shallow water near land, they slow down and pile up, growing into towering walls that can flood far inland. This is a tsunami. Often the sea pulls strangely far back from the beach just before the first wave arrives, exposing the bare seafloor. People who recognize that warning sign and run to high ground have a chance to survive."

A student claims: "A tsunami is dangerous because the earthquake's shaking knocks down buildings near the beach." Quote evidence from the passage that contradicts this explanation of the danger, and explain what the real cause is.
items.answer: Contradicting evidence: "When a big earthquake strikes near the coast, the danger is not over when the shaking stops." This shows the tsunami danger comes after the shaking, not from it. The real cause is the sudden movement of the seafloor pushing the water into waves that grow tall near shore and flood the land, so the shaking knocking down buildings is not what makes a tsunami dangerous.

steps: The student blames the shaking for the tsunami danger.
Find evidence showing the danger is separate from the shaking.
The sentence saying the danger is not over when shaking stops contradicts the claim.
Explain the real cause: seafloor movement pushes water into waves that grow tall near shore.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"In the early 1900s, a young woman named Bessie Coleman dreamed of flying, but no flight school in the United States would admit her because she was both Black and a woman. Rather than give up, she learned French, sailed to France, and earned her pilot's license there in 1921, becoming the first Black woman in the world to hold one. When she returned home, she performed daring stunts at air shows that drew huge crowds. Coleman refused to perform at any show that would not admit Black spectators alongside white ones. She used her fame to encourage other Black Americans, especially women, to take up flying. She hoped to open a flight school of her own so that no one would have to cross an ocean to learn as she had. Coleman died young in a flying accident before that dream came true, but the schools and clubs that later trained Black pilots often credited her example."

The central idea is that Coleman fought barriers and opened doors for others, not just for herself. Two quotations appear below. Choose the one that best supports the part of the central idea about opening doors for OTHERS, and explain why the other quotation supports a different point.

Quotation P: "She learned French, sailed to France, and earned her pilot's license there in 1921."
Quotation Q: "She used her fame to encourage other Black Americans, especially women, to take up flying."
items.answer: Best for opening doors for others: Quotation Q, "She used her fame to encourage other Black Americans, especially women, to take up flying." It directly shows her helping others enter aviation. Quotation P supports a different point, namely her own determination to overcome the barriers she personally faced, not how she opened doors for others.

steps: The central idea has two parts: she fought barriers and she helped others.
The question asks for evidence about helping others.
Quotation Q shows her encouraging other Black Americans to fly, which is about others.
Quotation P shows her own struggle to get licensed, supporting the personal-barrier part instead.
